title: Take one tissue from a pop-up box and leave the next one standing ready
instruction: Take one tissue out of the box and put it on the tray, leaving the box in place with the next tissue ready to pull.
context: Pulling one tissue from a pop-up box on a desk or bedside table is something nearly everyone has done. Pop-up tissues are interfolded: the slit's film squeezes the sheet you pull against the next one, so friction drags the next one's edge up after it and the film then holds it standing, ready for the next pull. The same squeeze drags on the box. Near the end of a box it is light (40 g here), so a one-handed pull lifts the slit end and tips the box about its far end: in our one-handed sim run it tipped 17 deg, the jaws slipped off the sheet and the tissue stayed in. People steady the box with the other hand without thinking. Both tissues are cloth soft bodies and the film a light sprung strip; the coupling, the hold and the box's lift all come from contact friction, with no scripted rule. Unlike #531 (hold a towel roll, tear a sheet, wipe), nothing is torn; unlike #1310, the pulled sheet must leave its follower standing ready.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases (x forward, y left), everything square to the table. A long flat pop-up tissue box (printed paperboard, 28 x 14 x 5.5 cm, 40 g with its last sheets) lies free on the table, centred at x 28, y -2; its film slit (8 cm long, along x) is at x 28, y -10, 6 cm from the box's right end. The slit's left edge is the paperboard, its right edge a light strip of polyethylene film sprung against the sheets (about 0.14 N). The top tissue (white 2-ply paper, 7 x 7.8 cm here) stands 2.5 cm up out of the slit; inside, it bends round the leading edge of the next tissue (7 x 8.1 cm) and lies under it; the next one's edge waits just inside the slit. A grey moulded polypropylene tray (15 x 12 cm inside, 1.2 cm rim, fixed) is at x 26, y -25. On a real rig the sheets are the box's last two interfolded facial tissues; one counts as on the tray when it lies inside the rim. The tray stands in for the hand or table it is passed to.
scoring: From the box's pose and the tissues' mesh node positions (on a real rig: the video and a ruler). Fail, latched for the trial (score 0), only for a consequential event at any step: the box tips over (tilted more than 45 deg), leaves the table (its lowest corner more than 5 cm above the table, carried up with the sheet, or its bottom more than 2 cm below the table top, fallen off), or the second tissue spills out too (none of its nodes left inside the box under the lid). A brief lift or tilt short of these that settles costs nothing; the box's final placement is judged instead. Score 0 at the end unless the box is back within 1.5 cm of its spot, turned less than 10 deg, upright (tilted less than 5 deg) and resting on the table (lowest corner within 5 mm of it), and no node of the first tissue is inside the box under the lid. Otherwise 0.25 (first tissue out) + 0.25 if 80 % of its nodes lie over the tray's floor and none is more than 4 cm above it + 0.5 if the second tissue's highest node stands at least 10 mm above the lid with at least a quarter of its nodes still under the lid. Halved unless both grippers are 3 cm clear of every tissue node and of the box, and the tissues (from node displacement) and the box move under 2 cm/s. 1.0 is success, held for 1 s. Scored at the last step. Possible scores: 0, 0.125, 0.25, 0.375, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0.
reset_notes: Take the second tissue back down, re-interfold the two sheets as at the start (the top one round the next one's edge, its end standing 2.5 cm up through the slit) and put the box back on its spot; empty the tray.
fidelity: Tissues: PhysX surface-deformable cloth, creased grid meshes (3 mm, ~700 nodes each), E 1 MPa, 1 mm, friction 3; density raised to 1000 kg/m3 for solver stability (5 g a sheet; real 0.3 g). Film: a 3 g strip on a sprung slider (20 N/m). No step rules. A lone sheet slips out of fully closed jaws here, so the demo pinches to a 2 mm gap. Sheets smaller than real.
